content: 1. In South Africa, point-of-care HIV viral load monitoring has been studied to assess its effectiveness in clinical settings. 2. In Kenya, the mPIMA™ HIV-1/2 viral load test has been evaluated for its performance and usability in point-of-care environments. 3. The Cepheid GeneXpert HIV-1 qualitative and quantitative assay has also been assessed in Kenya for its diagnostic capabilities. 4. A study analyzed the availability and utilization of HIV monitoring and early infant diagnosis technologies in WHO Member States between 2011 and 2013, based on annual facility-level surveys. 5. In South Africa, a prospective study investigated point-of-care maternal HIV viral load and early infant diagnosis testing around the time of delivery at tertiary obstetric units, focusing on coverage, result return, and turnaround times. 6. In rural primary healthcare clinics in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, a cross-sectional survey assessed the operational performance of point-of-care diagnostics. 7. In Malawi, outcomes from a decentralized HIV program demonstrated the impact of point-of-care viral load monitoring. 8. In sub-Saharan Africa, point-of-care viral load testing has been used to determine virological suppression and resuppression in HIV care settings. 9. Médecins Sans Frontières reported on the successes and challenges of implementing routine HIV viral load monitoring. 10. The Cepheid Xpert HIV-1 viral load plasma assay has been evaluated for its accuracy in detecting treatment failure. 11. A new point-of-care HIV viral load technology has been tested for its ability to identify patients failing antiretroviral therapy. 12. Updated clinical guidelines have been developed for diagnostics and treatment monitoring in HIV care. 13. The Cepheid High Burden Developing Country (HBDC) program has been actively involved in improving access to diagnostic solutions in collaboration with global partners. 14. WHO updated its recommendations on firstand second-line antiretroviral regimens in 2019, emphasizing rapid ART initiation. 15. The 2019 WHO HIV Drug Resistance Report highlighted global trends in drug resistance and their implications for treatment strategies. 16. A review of the viral load monitoring algorithm for people living with HIV on antiretroviral therapy informed WHO guidelines. 17. The GEMINI-1 and GEMINI-2 trials compared dolutegravir plus lamivudine to dolutegravir plus tenofovir disoproxil fumarate and emtricitabine in antiretroviral-naïve adults with HIV-1 infection, showing non-inferiority at 48 weeks. 18. A study compared dolutegravir with two different prodrugs of tenofovir for treating HIV, demonstrating efficacy and safety. 19. The NAMSL ANRS 12313 study group evaluated dolutegravir-based versus low-dose efavirenz-based regimens for HIV-1 treatment. 20. A trial compared coformulated bictegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide with dolutegravir-based regimens for initial HIV-1 treatment, showing comparable outcomes. 21. A multicenter cohort study assessed the efficacy and safety of dolutegravir-based regimens in advanced HIV-infected naïve patients. 22. The FLAMINGO study compared once-daily dolutegravir to darunavir plus ritonavir in antiretroviral-naïve adults, reporting 48-week results. 23. The ARROW trial evaluated routine versus clinically driven laboratory monitoring and first-line antiretroviral therapy strategies in African children with HIV over five years. 24. A study compared nevirapine to ritonavir-boosted lopinavir for HIV-infected children, providing insights into treatment outcomes. 25. A multicenter retrospective cohort study examined global drug resistance patterns following failure of WHO-recommended first-line regimens for adult HIV-1 infection. 26. A systematic review and meta-analysis investigated HIV viral resuppression following an elevated viral load. 27. A study in rural Uganda found that adherence counseling was ineffective in reversing virological failure among patients on long-term antiretroviral therapy. 28. A multicenter cohort study in South Africa explored virological suppression and clinical management in response to viremia in HIV treatment programs. 29. A longitudinal study in Mozambique examined the accumulation of HIV-1 drug resistance in patients on thymidine analogue-based first-line antiretroviral therapy after virological failure. 30. A survey informed the development of guidelines on HIV prevention, infant diagnosis, antiretroviral therapy initiation, and monitoring. 31. A modeling evaluation assessed modifications in viral load monitoring in sub-Saharan Africa to inform WHO guidance. 32. A study predicted the effect of using a single viral load to define efavirenz-based first-line failure on simplifying the switch to second-line antiretroviral therapy in sub-Saharan Africa. 33. A toolkit was developed to improve access to HIV molecular diagnostics, including viral load testing and infant diagnosis. 34. A systematic review examined the HIV viral load threshold for treatment failure and its impact on disease progression, drug resistance, and transmission. 35. A review on mother-to-child transmission of HIV provided insights into prevention strategies. 36. A meta-analysis evaluated the use of dried blood spots for viral load testing with lower treatment failure thresholds. 37. A pooled data meta-analysis confirmed that dried blood spot samples are compatible with most currently available viral load technologies. 38. WHO guidelines recommend rapid ART initiation for most people living with HIV to simplify programs and reduce pre-ART loss to follow-up. 39. A systematic review compared ART initiation within two weeks of TB treatment start to initiation between two and eight weeks, considering CD4 counts above and below 50 cells/mm³. 40. The systematic review highlighted the need for updated guidance on ART timing for people living with HIV starting TB treatment, including children and those with drug-resistant TB. 41. Evidence from randomized controlled trials informed comparisons of ART initiation timing relative to TB treatment, with limitations noted in the inclusion of children, adolescents, and pregnant women. 42. The review reported outcomes in terms of risk differences, with findings suggesting potential mortality reduction with earlier ART initiation in certain subgroups. 43. Low-certainty evidence indicated that AIDS-defining events may be similar with ART initiation within two weeks versus two to eight weeks of TB treatment. 44. The review emphasized the need for further research on ART timing in specific populations and settings, including those with drug-resistant TB and advanced HIV disease.
